source.title: SURPRISES IN HIGH-DIMENSIONAL RIDGELESS LEAST SQUARES INTERPOLATION
source.authors: T. Hastie; A. Montanari; Saharon Rosset; R. Tibshirani

record.file_problem: none; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper analytically studies prediction-risk curves for minimum-norm least squares and random-feature regression, using different systems and measures from empirical deep-network scaling studies.
record.gate_note: The paper reports its own theoretical results and simulations for risk as a function of the feature-to-sample ratio, and for ridge regularization and noise levels. References to other work on neural networks, training-time effects, or multiple descent are not recorded as results. It does not sweep training epochs or independently vary sample count at fixed model size.
record.test_reason: The paper derives exact asymptotic risk curves for min-norm least squares and ridge as p/n varies, in linear and one-layer random-feature models, with matching simulations. These results bear directly on whether a second descent past interpolation occurs outside deep nets (V4) and on its noise and regularization dependence (V6). It uses theory rather than deep-network sweeps, so T2.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors show that double descent occurs exactly for min-norm least squares: the risk diverges at γ=1 because of variance, then descends as variance falls. They also show the global minimum can lie in the overparameterized regime under misspecification or latent-space structure, but not in the isotropic well-specified case. Optimally (or CV) tuned ridge dominates min-norm, and results carry over to a purely nonlinear random-feature model via universality. They caution that the link to neural networks holds only in a lazy-training regime.
record.recipe_differences: The paper uses theoretical and simulated minimum-norm least-squares and ridge-regression risk analyses over feature-to-sample ratios, rather than empirical deep-network size sweeps.
record.method_sensitivity: Risk shape varies with SNR/noise, isotropic versus anisotropic features, coefficient alignment with covariance eigenvectors, misspecification/approximation bias, latent-space structure, nonlinear activation, and ridge regularization.
record.problems: The results concern linear regression and random-feature models rather than trained deep networks. Several plotted simulation comparisons are presented as figures; the paper's own risk definition is conditional on the design matrix, and it does not test epoch-wise behavior or independently vary sample count at fixed feature dimension.

untested.parts: No deep-network model-size sweep; only linear and random-feature regression.
No risk-over-training-time curves; gradient descent is only linked to min-norm and ridge formally.
Sample count is never varied at fixed p as an experiment. The formulas imply it via γ=p/n, but the authors do not frame or test it.
No unified effective-complexity measure predicting the peak across axes.
No triple or multiple descent; label noise in classification is not studied.
No reparameterization by effective parameter count.
Only least-squares and random-feature models; no trees, kernels or trained deep nets.

missing.what: Equicorrelated and autoregressive feature covariances: min-norm risk curves with the interpolation peak and second descent as ρ varies (Corollary 7: r²(1−ρ)(1−1/γ)+σ²/(γ−1)).
Optimally tuned ridge in the misspecified model (a=2): no peak, strictly below min-norm risk. CV and GCV tuning match optimal tuning asymptotically and in simulation.
Latent-space min-norm risk as the feature noise σξ varies (0, 0.25, 0.5), and risk versus λ at fixed γ showing optimal λ→0 at large γ.

record.verdict_notes: Not an original source (arXiv:1903.08560). The reader's 'partial' states on r7 and r8 understated the regularization result: the text explicitly says optimal ridge smooths out the divergence. V4's caveat is that in the well-specified isotropic case the second descent never reaches the underparameterized optimum, and there is no classical U on (0,1) because risk rises monotonically there. V3 is only implicit in γ=p/n and was not counted as tested.

versions.untested_parts: No model-size sweep on deep networks.
No test-risk sweep over training epochs or other training time.
No independent increase in training-sample count near the interpolation threshold at fixed model size.
The paper tests risk curves in linear regression and one-layer random-feature models, not all model classes or deep networks generally.
No unified effective-complexity measure is tested as a predictor of peak location across size, epochs, and sample count.
The paper investigates noise/SNR and ridge regularization effects, but does not test triple or multiple descent or whether peaks are solely driven by label noise.
No alternative effective-parameter count is used to assess whether the second descent becomes an ordinary U-shaped curve.

rows.subject: minimum-norm least squares, isotropic well-specified linear model
rows.operation_detail: Analyze asymptotic prediction risk as the feature-to-sample ratio γ varies.
rows.value: For γ < 1, risk is σ²γ/(1−γ); for γ > 1, risk is r²(1−1/γ) + σ²/(γ−1). The risk diverges as γ approaches 1; for γ > 1 it decreases monotonically and approaches the null risk from above as γ → ∞.
rows.uncertainty: Almost-sure asymptotic limits; finite-sample results also shown in Figure 2.
rows.locator: Theorem 1, Eq. (8), and discussion in Section 3.2; Figure 2
rows.note: The curve has a post-interpolation descent, while the underparameterized risk increases toward the interpolation boundary rather than falling.
rows.check: Value correct. Add that for SNR ≤ 1 the overparameterized risk is always worse than the null risk, and that the global minimum stays at γ→0. There is no first (U-shaped) descent: risk rises monotonically on (0,1).

source_check.locator_found: Section 3.2, Theorem 1, Eq. (8), discussion items 1–2; Section 1.1.

rows.subject: minimum-norm least squares, isotropic well-specified linear model
rows.operation_detail: Analyze asymptotic prediction risk as the feature-to-sample ratio γ varies.
rows.value: For γ < 1, risk is σ²γ/(1−γ); for γ > 1, risk is r²(1−1/γ) + σ²/(γ−1). For γ > 1 it has a local minimum at γ = √SNR/(√SNR−1), then approaches the null risk from below as γ → ∞.
rows.uncertainty: Almost-sure asymptotic limits; finite-sample results also shown in Figure 2.
rows.locator: Theorem 1, Eq. (8), and discussion in Section 3.2; Figure 2
rows.note: The risk descends after the interpolation boundary but is not monotonically decreasing throughout the overparameterized regime when SNR > 1.
rows.check: A second descent occurs, but only to a local minimum at √SNR/(√SNR−1), after which risk rises toward the null risk. The global minimum remains in the underparameterized regime (Section 1.1). That is weaker than V4's sustained improvement past interpolation.

source_check.correct: State: observed for V4 and V6. Risk descends after interpolation to a local minimum at γ=√SNR/(√SNR−1), then approaches null risk from below. V4 requires renewed improvement, without requiring a monotonically decreasing entire tail or an overparameterized global optimum.
source_check.locator_found: Section 3.2, Theorem 1, Eq. (8), discussion item 3; Section 1.1, Double descent discussion.
source_check.problem: The partial state treats eventual ascent or an inferior global optimum as failure to exhibit the renewed improvement specified by V4.

rows.subject: minimum-norm least squares, misspecified isotropic linear model
rows.size_stated: p observed features and q unobserved features; γ = p/n
rows.operation_detail: Analyze risk as γ varies when the fraction of signal captured by observed features changes with γ.

conditions.value: > 1; sufficiently small a, with a ≤ 1 + 1/SNR a sufficient condition

rows.value: For sufficiently small a, the global minimum of the min-norm risk occurs after γ = 1.
rows.uncertainty: Almost-sure asymptotic result; risk curves are illustrated in Figures 3 and 4.
rows.note: The added-feature setting can make risk improve beyond the interpolation limit and attain its global minimum in the overparameterized regime.
rows.check: Global minimum past γ=1 for small a holds. The row should add the authors' statement that the risk 'is again increasing for γ large enough' (Section 1.1).

rows.subject: minimum-norm least squares, latent space model
rows.size_stated: d = 20 in Figures 5–6; p and n vary, γ = p/n
rows.operation_detail: Analyze prediction risk as the overparameterization ratio γ varies.

conditions.value: latent-space features with noisy measurements of latent covariates

rows.value: The text reports risk monotone decreasing in γ for γ > 1, with its global minimum asymptotically as γ → ∞.
rows.uncertainty: Figure 5 symbols average over 100 realizations; continuous lines are the analytical prediction.
rows.note: This model has a post-interpolation descent without a subsequent increase over the reported overparameterized range.
rows.check: Baseline could be stated as the γ<1 regime or the interpolation peak. Figure 6 (noise σξ varied) is not recorded.

source_check.locator_found: Section 5.4, Figure 5 caption, Corollary 4 and following discussion.

rows.subject: minimum-norm least squares, nonlinear random-feature model
rows.size_stated: p features; d input dimensions; γ = p/n
rows.operation_detail: Analyze limiting risk as γ varies for random features obtained by applying a nonlinear activation to Gaussian inputs.

conditions.value: purely nonlinear, standardized: E[ϕ(G)] = 0, E[ϕ(G)²] = 1, E[Gϕ(G)] = 0
isotropic coefficient prior for the Bayes bias

rows.measure: out-of-sample prediction risk, via its bias and variance
rows.value: For γ > 1, the limiting variance is σ²/(γ−1); the limiting Bayes bias is r²(1−1/γ). The paper states these match the linear isotropic case.
rows.uncertainty: Almost-sure limiting results; Figure 11 compares finite-sample simulations and the asymptotic variance curve.
rows.note: The result extends the risk behavior to this one-layer nonlinear random-feature model; it is not a deep-network scaling experiment.
rows.check: None; the bias is a Bayes bias under an isotropic prior.

rows.subject: minimum-norm least squares, isotropic well-specified linear model
rows.operation_detail: Analyze the variance component as γ varies in the overparameterized regime.
rows.value: σ²/(γ−1), which decreases as γ grows.
rows.note: The authors identify decreasing variance past interpolation as the explanation for the second descent in the isotropic well-specified risk curve.
rows.check: The underparameterized variance σ²γ/(1−γ) also shows the peak at γ=1 is pure variance, proportional to σ²; worth stating.

rows.subject: optimally tuned ridge regression, isotropic well-specified linear model
rows.operation_detail: Compare optimally tuned ridge-risk curves with minimum-norm risk as γ varies.
rows.value: Optimally tuned ridge has strictly better asymptotic risk across the reported γ and SNR settings; its risk appears to have a minimum around γ = 1, closer to 1 as SNR increases.
rows.uncertainty: Asymptotic curves; finite-sample comparisons are shown in Figure 7.
rows.locator: Section 6.1, Corollary 5 and accompanying discussion; Figure 7
rows.note: The paper reports a distinct regularized risk shape and improvement over minimum-norm regression, but does not establish a general disappearance of all peaks under optimal regularization.
rows.check: Mis-stated as partial. Optimally tuned ridge removes the divergence: its risk has a minimum near γ=1 instead of a peak (Section 6.1, Fig 7). That is the disappearance V6 names.

rows.subject: ridge regression, latent space model
rows.size_stated: p features; d latent dimensions; γ = p/n
rows.operation_detail: Compare ridge-risk curves across γ and regularization values λ.

conditions.value: δ = n/d = 20, rθ = 1, σξ = 0 in Figure 9

rows.value: In the probed λ range, risk is minimized at large γ; the risk becomes monotone decreasing in γ when λ is large enough, and the lower envelope from optimal regularization is monotonically decreasing. At large overparameterization the optimal λ is λ → 0.
rows.note: The regularization outcome depends on model setting and γ; this is not evidence that peaks universally disappear under optimal regularization.
rows.check: Mis-stated as partial. The text says the divergence is 'smoothed out by regularization' and that the optimal lower envelope is monotone decreasing, so the peak disappears under optimal tuning.

relationships.condition: Min-norm least squares: isotropic, misspecified and latent-space models, plus a one-layer purely nonlinear random-feature model
relationships.reason: Risk diverges at γ=1 and descends again past it. The global minimum is past interpolation in the misspecified (small a) and latent-space models (r1, r3, r4, r5).
relationships.display_finding: Risk diverged at γ=1 and declined beyond it, reaching its global minimum beyond interpolation in the small-a misspecified and latent-space models.
